rules.title: 5 rules from UC's own guide

facts.text: Each answer can be up to 350 words.
Favorite questions. No question helps or hurts you. They're numbered, not ranked.
Most of each answer should be about the present or recent past.
Readers look at what you say about yourself, not your style or structure.

rules.note: Good news: they're not grading your sentences.
rules.src: Source: University of California, Personal Insight Questions guide for counselors (fall 2025 first-year edition). Check UC's site for anything that changes.

take.heading: What I saw as an admissions reader
take.quote: The answers I remember were never the fanciest. They were the most specific: one real Saturday, one real number, one thing you actually did. UC says it out loud: they read for facts about you. So fill every blank with something only you could write.

lede.s: Fill in just the first blank on all 8 cards. The 4 where real details came fastest are your 4. Tap ☆ on those cards.
lede.p: Have your student fill in just the first blank on all 8 cards. The 4 where real details came fastest are their 4. Tap ☆ on those cards.

cards.prompt: Describe an example of your leadership experience in which you have positively influenced others, helped resolve disputes or contributed to group efforts over time.
cards.uc_says: You don't need a definition of leadership, and it isn't asking about titles.
cards.ask: Ask your student: when did you step up when nobody asked you to?
cards.frame: In {a group, team, family or job you're part of}, {the moment that needed someone: one real day or problem}. I stepped up by {what you did: 2 or 3 action verbs}. The hard part was {what made it hard}. Because of it, {what changed, with a number if you can}. Now I {how you lead or help now}.

fills: my aunt's taco truck on weekends
our card reader died on a Saturday with 20 people in line
taking cash, writing orders on paper plates and sending my cousin to the bank for change
nobody put me in charge. My aunt was cooking and I'm 16
we didn't lose one order. Now we keep a backup cash box and a printed price list
train the 2 new weekend workers, and my robotics team calls me when a plan falls apart
example.note: No title needed. Just a real Saturday.

cards.prompt: Every person has a creative side, and it can be expressed in many ways: problem solving, original and innovative thinking, and artistically, to name a few. Describe how you express your creative side.
cards.uc_says: Don't box in your idea of creative. A smart fix counts as much as art.
cards.ask: Ask your student: what's a problem you solved in a way nobody else would have?
cards.frame: The problem was {a real problem you had to solve}. The obvious fix was {what most people would do}, but I tried {your different idea} instead. Here's what happened: {the result}. I use that same kind of thinking now when I {where it shows up today}.

fills: my little brother would not practice reading
flash cards and a timer
writing a comic about his dog, one page a night, where he had to read the speech bubbles out loud to find out what happened
we finished 41 pages, and his teacher moved him up a reading group in March
plan lessons for the kids I tutor at the library on Tuesdays
example.note: Creative doesn't have to mean art.

cards.prompt: What would you say is your greatest talent or skill? How have you developed and demonstrated that talent over time?
cards.uc_says: List your skills first, then pick the one that means the most. Focus on how it shows up now.
cards.ask: Ask your student: what do people come to you for?
cards.frame: Things I'm good at: {skill 1}, {skill 2} and {skill 3}. The one that matters most to me is {pick one} because {why it matters}. It {came naturally, or took work}: {how you built it}. Proof from this year: {one specific moment, with a number if you can}.

fills: fixing phones
making people laugh
translating Spanish and English
translating
my family counts on it for real things, like doctor visits and our lease
took work
I keep a notebook of medical and money words I didn't know. It's 6 pages now
I translated at 9 of my grandma's appointments, and now I help at the clinic front desk on Thursdays

cards.prompt: Describe how you have taken advantage of a significant educational opportunity or worked to overcome an educational barrier you have faced.
cards.uc_says: You're not being compared to other students. This gives readers context for your grades and classes.
cards.ask: Ask your student: what did you go out and find that your school didn't offer?
cards.frame: At my school, {what was missing, or what was offered}. So I {what you did: a program, mentor, online class or community college class}. It cost me {what you gave up: time, sleep, a shift at work}. What I got out of it: {what you learned or can do now}. You can see it in my transcript as {the class, grade or credit}.

fills: there's no computer science class
took Intro to Python at our community college 2 nights a week, 2 buses each way
my Tuesday and Thursday shifts at the grocery store
I can build programs that work. I made the sign-up sheet our school food pantry uses
Intro to Python, an A, on my community college transcript

cards.prompt: Describe the most significant challenge you have faced and the steps you have taken to overcome this challenge. How has this challenge affected your academic achievement?
cards.uc_says: It can be personal. Share only what you want to. But say how it affected your schoolwork.
cards.ask: Ask gently and let them choose what to share: what's been hardest, and how did it affect school?
cards.frame: The hardest thing I've faced is {one honest sentence. Share only what you want to}. It hit my schoolwork when {what happened to grades, attendance or focus}. The steps I took: {what you did, in order}. Where I am now: {how school is going now}. What I know about myself because of it: {what you learned}.

fills: my family moved 3 times in 2 years, so I changed high schools twice
I missed most of Algebra 2 at my old school and got a D first semester
I asked for the class notes on day one, went to lunch tutoring 3 days a week and retook the unit tests
I got a B+ in Precalculus this year
I don't wait until I'm behind anymore. I ask on day one
example.note: Tie it back to school. That's the question.

cards.prompt: Think about an academic subject that inspires you. Describe how you have furthered this interest inside and/or outside of the classroom.
cards.uc_says: The subject doesn't have to be a core class. Say how it connects to what you want to study.
cards.ask: Ask your student: what class or topic do you keep thinking about after the bell?
cards.frame: I got hooked on {a subject} when {one specific class, book, problem or moment}. Outside of class, I {what you did on your own}. It connects to {a major or career you're thinking about} because {why it matters to you}. The question I still want to answer: {a real question}

fills: chemistry
we figured out why my mom's bread kept coming out flat. It was the yeast and the water temperature
keep a baking log with temperatures and results. I'm at 30 loaves
food science
I want to make food that's cheap, healthy and still tastes good
why does gluten-free bread fall apart, and can I fix it?
example.note: One real moment beats "I've always loved…"

cards.prompt: What have you done to make your school or your community a better place?
cards.uc_says: Small changes count. If it was a group, focus on your part. Readers can't click links.
cards.ask: Ask your student: what's one thing you made better, even a small thing?
cards.frame: I noticed {a problem at your school or in your community}. It bothered me because {why you cared}. My part, not the group's, was {your specific jobs}. What changed: {the result. Small counts}. What I learned: {one thing you'd do again or do differently}.

fills: kids at my school skipped lunch because the line took 20 minutes
my friends were buying chips from the vending machine instead of eating
timing the line for 2 weeks, making a chart and presenting it to our principal
they opened a second line in January, and the wait is about 8 minutes now
numbers get adults to listen faster than complaints do

cards.prompt: Beyond what has already been shared in your application, what do you believe makes you a strong candidate for admissions to the University of California?
cards.uc_says: Use it to explain or add to what's already in your application. Don't send extra documents.
cards.ask: Ask your student: what should a reader know that isn't on your transcript?
cards.frame: Something readers won't see anywhere else in my application: {a fact about your life}. On a normal school day, I also {what fills your time outside class}. One thing in my application that needs context is {a grade, gap or empty spot}, because {the reason}. What all of this says about me as a student: {one sentence}.

fills: I take care of my 2 younger sisters every day after school until 7
make dinner and check their homework, then start mine at 8
my junior year has no sports or clubs
my after-school hours go to my sisters
I'm organized, and I finish what I start

title.s: Before you paste them into UC's application
title.p: Before your student pastes them into UC's application

lede.s: Tap each one you can say yes to, for all 4 answers.
lede.p: Your student taps each one they can say yes to, for all 4 answers.

items.title: Most of it is about now
items.body: Most of each answer is about the present or the last year or two. One line of backstory is plenty.

items.title: Every blank is only-you
items.body: Could another student paste your blank into their answer? If yes, add a place, a day or a number.

items.title: You said what you did
items.body: In group stories, readers need your part. Swap some "we" for "I."

items.title: #5 ties back to school
items.body: If you picked the challenge question, you said how it affected your schoolwork and what you did about it.

items.title: 4 different sides
items.body: Your 4 answers show 4 different sides of you, not the same story 4 times.

items.title: No links, no "see my resume"
items.body: Readers can't click links or look you up. Everything they need is in your words.

self_check.all_done: 6 of 6. Read all 4 out loud once, then paste them in.

after.s: Not there yet? That's normal. Fix one thing at a time.
after.p: Not there yet? That's normal. Help them fix one thing at a time.
